place.zh: 银叶谷 · 石洞 · 夜
place.en: The Silver-leaf Vale · a cave · night

_weather: 「蘸着雨水」「只听见雨」 until 「快到天亮的时候，雨停了」 at its end

setup.zh: 崖壁下一个浅石洞。你生起一小堆火挡在洞口，怀里是阿禾的鸡蛋和娘烙的那张厚饼。
setup.en: A shallow cave under the cliff. You light a small fire across the mouth; inside your jacket, Ahe's egg and the thick flatbread your mother made.

recap.zh: 石洞里生了火，你把吃的分给它，给它擦伤口；睡着前，有人说：本王记住你了。
recap.en: In the cave you lit a fire, shared your food with the fox and cleaned its wounds; as you fell asleep someone said: this queen will remember you.

zh: 怀里两样东西：一个煮鸡蛋，一张厚饼。
en: A shallow cave, a small fire.
The resin crackles; no beast comes near.
Two things in your jacket: a boiled egg, a thick flatbread.

story.zh:
他在崖壁底下找到了一个浅浅的石洞，先往里扔了一块石头，听了听，是空的；又扔了一块，又听了听，还是空的；待要再捡第三块，想想算了，还是进去了。

他用他爹教的法子，拿那把火镰敲着火石，引着了干苔和松脂，生了一小堆火，火堆挡在洞口，野兽便不敢进来。

然后他从怀里摸出了两样东西：阿禾给的煮鸡蛋，和他娘给的那张厚饼——沈家最后的一点白面。
story.en:
At the foot of the cliff he found a shallow cave. First he threw a stone in and listened: empty. He threw another and listened again: still empty. He was about to pick up a third, then thought better of it and went in.

Using the way his father had taught him, he struck the flint with the fire steel, lit some dry moss and pine resin, and got a little fire going. With a fire across the mouth of the cave, animals wouldn't dare come in.

Then he took two things out of his jacket: the boiled egg Ahe had given him, and the thick flatbread from his mother — the last of the Shens' white flour.

exits.means: shares the egg and the bread with the fox, feeds it

story.zh:
他把鸡蛋剥了，掰了一半放在它嘴边，它闻了闻，看了他一眼，才慢慢地吃了下去。小满心里暗暗叫苦：阿禾，对不起。这个鸡蛋的利息，只怕要还三个了。

跟着是饼。他把自己那一半掰下一大块来，放在它嘴边，剩下一个小角包好了，留作明天的早饭。它吃完了，舔了舔嘴，把脑袋一扭，闭上了眼睛，连个谢字也没有。

天黑透了没多久，它却发起烧来。他爹说过，山里的活物受了重伤，头一夜总要发烧，熬过去就活，熬不过去就不活。守火的人不能睡，想来想去，只有一个法子能叫自己不睡着，便是说话。

说到马小宝，他道：「他手里永远捏着一块桂花糕。桂花糕是什么味儿，我到现在都不知道。闻着是香的。你吃过吗？——哦，你是狐狸，你吃鸡。」说到桂花糕的时候，它的耳朵动了一下。

「我家的人都这样，」他说，「谁疼了，都不说疼。我家的规矩，疼了不说，也没人问。问了，就得答；答了，就得哭；哭了，饭就凉了。」

他抱着柴钻回洞里，把火重新拨旺，一回头，却见它躺在那里，一动不动了。他捧着它，冲它嚷：「你吃了我家最后的白面！你吃了阿禾的鸡蛋！你咬了我一口！你这一死，这几笔账，我找谁要去？」

过了好一会儿，它的胸口，轻轻地，鼓了一下。又鼓了一下。快到天亮的时候，雨停了。他伸手去摸它，它身上不烫了。

他实在太累了，抱着它靠在石壁上，不知什么时候便睡着了。睡着之前，他好像听见有人在他耳边，用很小很小的声音说了一句话——不是狐狸叫，是人话，是一个姑娘的声音，带着几分不情不愿：⟪「……凡人。本王记住你了。」⟫
story.en:
He peeled the egg, broke off half, and put it by the fox's mouth. It sniffed it, looked at him, and only then slowly ate it. Xiaoman groaned to himself: Ahe, I'm sorry. The interest on this egg is going to be three, at least.

Then came the flatbread. He broke a big piece off his own half and put it by its mouth, wrapped up the small corner that was left, to save for tomorrow's breakfast. The fox finished, licked its lips, turned its head away and shut its eyes, without so much as a thank-you.

Not long after full dark the fox ran a fever. His father had said that when a creature in the mountains is badly hurt, it always runs a fever the first night: get through it and you live, don't and you don't. Whoever keeps the fire can't sleep. He thought and thought, and there was only one way to keep himself awake, and that was to talk.

When he got to Ma Xiaobao he said, "He's always got a piece of osmanthus cake in his hand. I still don't know what osmanthus cake tastes like. It smells nice. Have you ever had any? — Oh, you're a fox. You eat chickens." At the words "osmanthus cake" its ear twitched.

"That's how everyone in my family is," he said. "When somebody hurts, nobody says it hurts. In our family, the rule is: if it hurts, you don't say so, and nobody asks. If they ask, you have to answer; if you answer, you'll cry; if you cry, the food goes cold."

He ducked back into the cave with the wood, stirred the fire up again, turned round — and saw it lying there, not moving at all. Holding it, he shouted at it: "You ate my family's last white flour! You ate Ahe's egg! You bit me! If you die, who am I supposed to collect those debts from?"

After a good while, its chest, gently, swelled once. And swelled again. Towards dawn the rain stopped. He reached out and felt it. It wasn't hot any more.

He was worn out. Holding it, he leaned back against the rock and at some point fell asleep. Just before he fell asleep, he thought he heard someone say something by his ear in a very, very small voice — not a fox's cry, but people talk, a girl's voice, rather grudging: ⟪"…Mortal. This queen will remember you."⟫

story_full.zh:
他把鸡蛋剥了，掰了一半放在它嘴边，它闻了闻，看了他一眼，才慢慢地吃了下去。他想了一想，把另一半也放在它嘴边，它闻了闻，又看了他一眼，又吃了。小满心里暗暗叫苦：阿禾，对不起。这个鸡蛋的利息，只怕要还三个了。

跟着是饼。他把饼掰成两半，一半给它，一半自己拿着。他饿了一整天，那半张饼在他手里，重得像一块金子。它把它那一半吃完了，便看着他手里这一半，又看了他一眼。他看着它，它看着他，火堆「噼啪」响了一声。

他把自己那一半掰下一大块来，放在它嘴边，剩下一个小角包好了，塞进包袱最底下，留作明天的早饭。它吃完了，舔了舔嘴，把脑袋一扭，闭上了眼睛，连个谢字也没有。

他撕下一片衣摆，蘸着雨水，一点一点地给它擦伤口上的泥。它不咬他了，只是在他碰到疼处时，耳朵往后一压，小小地「呜」一声。火光里，他瞧见它的伤口正在慢慢地、慢慢地合拢。

伤口是合拢了，天黑透了没多久，它却发起烧来。隔着那件旧外衣，一股热气一阵一阵地透将出来，烫得他手心发汗。他把衣裳掀开一角，只见它蜷得更紧了，鼻头干得起了皮，喘气又短又急，一口气到了喉咙口便折回来，像一只拉破了的风箱。

他爹说过，山里的活物受了重伤，头一夜总要发烧，熬过去就活，熬不过去就不活。

这句话他记得很清楚，因为他爹说完了，又补了一句：「人也一样。」

他没有药，只有雨水。他把那片衣摆撕成两块，一块蘸湿了搭在它脑门上，另一块伸到洞口去接雨，等这一块捂热了，便换那一块。守火的人不能睡，睡着了，火就灭了。想来想去，只有一个法子能叫自己不睡着，便是说话。

洞里没有别人，只有一只狐狸，那便跟它说。他自己浑身也是湿的，外衣又裹在它身上，冷得牙齿直打架，便把身子往火边挪了又挪。

他本想先告诉它自己叫什么，想了一想，一只狐狸，记住了也没处写，便省了。他跟它说他娘那十七个盆，说他爹那只会聊天的膝盖，说后天就是立冬，马三要来拿他爷爷的弓，还说那叫父债子偿。

说到马小宝，他道：「他手里永远捏着一块桂花糕。桂花糕是什么味儿，我到现在都不知道。闻着是香的。你吃过吗？——哦，你是狐狸，你吃鸡。」说到桂花糕的时候，它的耳朵动了一下。他只当是烧得难受，一只狐狸，哪里听得懂人话。

他又跟它说那只碗，在半空里翻了两个筋斗，他伸手去捞，差了一寸。

「我家的人都这样，」他说，「谁疼了，都不说疼。我爹的膝盖疼，他说它在聊天；我娘蹲在地上捡碗，她什么都不说；我摔成这样，我也不说。我家的规矩，疼了不说，也没人问。问了，就得答；答了，就得哭；哭了，饭就凉了。」

说完这几句，他起身换了一回布，它身上还是烫的。

到了半夜，火堆矮了下去。他猫着腰钻出洞去，摸到崖根底下折了几根枯枝，每折一根，满树的银叶子便「叮叮」地响成一片，好像在骂人。

他只得小声道：「对不住，借两根。明儿还你。」他抱着柴，竖起耳朵往崖上听，只听见雨，别的什么也听不见。他爹的耳朵，听得见三里外的獐子；他的耳朵，只是一般。

他抱着柴钻回洞里，把火重新拨旺，一回头，却见它躺在那里，一动不动了。

他脑子里「嗡」的一声，扑过去把它捧了起来。它身上还烫着，可胸口那一起一伏，他瞧了半天，竟瞧不出来。他把耳朵贴到它身上听，什么也听不见，只听见自己的心在怦怦乱跳。

他捧着它，手足无措，平日里一张嘴能说会道，这时候翻来覆去，只说得出一句：「喂。喂。你别——」说到这里，不知怎的，他又算起账来，一面算，一面冲它嚷：「你吃了我家最后的白面！你吃了阿禾的鸡蛋！你咬了我一口！你这一死，这几笔账，我找谁要去？」

他嚷完了，洞里静悄悄的，只有火「噼啪」响了一声。过了好一会儿——也许只有一口气那么长，他却觉得比一整夜还长——它的胸口，轻轻地，鼓了一下。又鼓了一下。他捧着它坐倒在地下，半天说不出话来，后背上全是冷汗。

从那以后，他便不敢停嘴了，倒像他一停，它那口气便也要跟着停。

他把这十二年的事翻来覆去说了个遍，说到后来，自己也不知道在说些什么，只是嘴不停，手也不停，换布，添柴，再换布，再添柴。快到天亮的时候，雨停了。

他伸手去摸它，它身上不烫了，喘气也匀了，一下一下，又长又稳，跟坑里那一点银光一明一暗的样子一模一样。

他实在太累了，抱着它靠在石壁上，不知什么时候便睡着了。睡着之前，他好像听见有人在他耳边，用很小很小的声音说了一句话——不是狐狸叫，是人话，是一个姑娘的声音，带着几分不情不愿：⟪「……凡人。本王记住你了。」⟫
story_full.en:
He peeled the egg, broke off half, and put it by the fox's mouth. It sniffed it, looked at him, and only then slowly ate it. He thought about it, then put the other half by its mouth too. It sniffed, looked at him again, and ate that as well. Xiaoman groaned to himself: Ahe, I'm sorry. The interest on this egg is going to be three, at least.

Then came the flatbread. He broke it in two, gave half to the fox, and kept half himself. He'd been hungry all day, and the half flatbread in his hand was as heavy as a lump of gold. The fox finished its half and looked at the half in his hand, then looked at him. He looked at it; it looked at him; the fire crackled.

He broke a big piece off his own half and put it by its mouth, wrapped up the small corner that was left, and stuffed it into the very bottom of his bundle, to save for tomorrow's breakfast. The fox finished, licked its lips, turned its head away and shut its eyes, without so much as a thank-you.

He tore a strip off the hem of his shirt, wet it with rainwater, and bit by bit cleaned the mud out of its wounds. It didn't bite him any more. Only, when he touched a sore place, its ears would flatten back and it would give a small whimper. In the firelight he saw its wounds closing, slowly, slowly.

The wounds closed; but not long after full dark the fox ran a fever. Through the old jacket, heat came off it in waves, hot enough to make his palms sweat. He lifted a corner of the cloth and saw it curled up tighter than ever, the skin on its nose dry and flaking, its breath short and fast, each breath reaching its throat and turning back, like a torn pair of bellows.

His father had said that when a creature in the mountains is badly hurt, it always runs a fever the first night: get through it and you live, don't and you don't.

He remembered that very clearly, because when his father had said it he'd added: "Same with people."

He had no medicine, only rainwater. He tore the strip of hem into two pieces. One he soaked and laid on the fox's forehead; the other he held out at the mouth of the cave to catch the rain, and when the first one warmed up he swapped it for the second. Whoever keeps the fire can't sleep; fall asleep, and the fire goes out. He thought and thought, and there was only one way to keep himself awake, and that was to talk.

There was nobody else in the cave, only a fox, so he talked to the fox. He was soaked through himself, and his jacket was wrapped round the fox, so he was so cold his teeth chattered, and he kept shifting closer and closer to the fire.

He'd meant to start by telling it his name, then thought: a fox — even if it remembered, it would have nowhere to write it down. So he skipped that. He told it about his mother's seventeen basins; about his father's knee that could chat; that the first day of winter was the day after tomorrow, and Ma San was coming to take his grandpa's bow, and that this was called a son paying his father's debts.

When he got to Ma Xiaobao he said, "He's always got a piece of osmanthus cake in his hand. I still don't know what osmanthus cake tastes like. It smells nice. Have you ever had any? — Oh, you're a fox. You eat chickens." At the words "osmanthus cake" its ear twitched. He thought it was just the fever bothering it. A fox — how could it understand people talk?

He told it about the bowl, too: how it turned two somersaults in the air, and he grabbed for it, and was an inch short.

"That's how everyone in my family is," he said. "When somebody hurts, nobody says it hurts. Pa's knee hurts, and he says it's chatting. Ma crouches on the floor picking up the bowl and doesn't say anything. I'm all smashed up like this, and I'm not saying anything either. In our family, the rule is: if it hurts, you don't say so, and nobody asks. If they ask, you have to answer; if you answer, you'll cry; if you cry, the food goes cold."

When he'd said that, he got up and changed the cloth again. The fox was still hot.

Around midnight the fire burned low. He ducked out of the cave, felt his way to the foot of the cliff and snapped off a few dead branches. Every branch he snapped set the whole tree's silver leaves *tinging* all together, as if they were telling him off.

He could only say, quietly, "Sorry. Just borrowing a couple. I'll give them back tomorrow." With the wood in his arms he pricked up his ears towards the top of the cliff and listened. All he could hear was the rain; nothing else. His father's ears could hear a river deer three li off. His own ears were only ordinary.

He ducked back into the cave with the wood, stirred the fire up again, turned round — and saw it lying there, not moving at all.

His head went *hummm*. He threw himself down and scooped it up. It was still hot, but the rise and fall of its chest — he looked and looked, and couldn't see it. He put his ear against it and listened, and couldn't hear a thing, only his own heart hammering away.

Holding it, he didn't know what to do with his hands or feet. On an ordinary day he had an answer for everything, and now, round and round, the only thing he could get out was: "Hey. Hey. Don't you—" And then, somehow, he started doing sums again, and as he did them he shouted at it: "You ate my family's last white flour! You ate Ahe's egg! You bit me! If you die, who am I supposed to collect those debts from?"

When he'd finished shouting, the cave was dead quiet. The fire crackled once. After a good while — maybe only as long as one breath, though to him it felt longer than a whole night — its chest, gently, swelled once. And swelled again. Holding it, he sat down hard on the ground and couldn't speak for a long time. His back was soaked in cold sweat.

After that he didn't dare stop talking, as if, if he stopped, its breath would stop with him.

He went over his whole twelve years again and again, and by the end he didn't know what he was saying himself; only his mouth didn't stop and his hands didn't stop: change the cloth, add wood, change the cloth again, add wood again. Towards dawn the rain stopped.

He reached out and felt it. It wasn't hot any more, and its breathing had evened out, one breath after another, long and steady, exactly like that point of silver light in the hollow, glowing and dimming.

He was worn out. Holding it, he leaned back against the rock and at some point fell asleep. Just before he fell asleep, he thought he heard someone say something by his ear in a very, very small voice — not a fox's cry, but people talk, a girl's voice, rather grudging: ⟪"…Mortal. This queen will remember you."⟫

refuse.en: The bread still hangs on its vines — get it down to the fox first.

exits.means: keeps the food, eats it alone

story.zh:
小满把那个剥了壳的鸡蛋，自己吃了。饼，他掰下一大半，也塞进了嘴里；剩下一个小角，包好了，塞进包袱最底下，留作明天的早饭。

这不叫小气，这叫算账。他饿了一整天，明天还不知道有没有吃的。

它在他的衣裳里看着他，一直看着，没出声。他给看得有点心虚，撕下一片衣摆，蘸着雨水，一点一点地给它擦伤口上的泥。它不咬他了，只是在他碰到疼处时，耳朵往后一压。

他太累了，抱着它靠在石壁上，不知什么时候便睡着了。睡着之前，他好像听见有人在他耳边，用很小很小的声音说了一句话，是一个姑娘的声音，带着几分不情不愿：⟪「……凡人。小气。——本王记住你了。」⟫
story.en:
Xiaoman ate the peeled egg himself. The flatbread — he broke off the larger part and stuffed that in his mouth too; the little corner left over he wrapped and tucked at the bottom of his bundle, for tomorrow's breakfast.

That wasn't stinginess; that was keeping accounts. He'd been hungry all day, and tomorrow there might be nothing to eat at all.

Inside his jacket it watched him — kept watching, without a sound. The watching made him feel a little guilty; he tore a strip from his hem, wet it with rainwater, and bit by bit wiped the mud from its wounds. It didn't bite him any more; only when he touched a sore place its ears went flat.

He was too tired. Holding it, he leaned against the rock wall and at some point fell asleep. Just before he slept he seemed to hear someone speak in his ear, very, very softly — a girl's voice, a little grudging: ⟪"…Mortal. Stingy. — This queen will remember you."⟫

_beats: 喂饼 (bread-share): since 2026-10-16 a 割绳子-style puzzle (games/bread.js, levels in games.json) — cut the vines so the 饼 reaches the fox; corners caught are stars. Its win always feeds the fox, so its grade is half (a corner saved) or most (all to it) and takes 分它一半; 自己吃 (none · little, from the 10-14 piece-by-piece board) opens only when the board is left (「算了，往下走」 opens every way). The task's marks keep the grade (bread-half · bread-most) for the 恩仇簿 and 「本王欠你一张饼」. The corner is always kept: the dawn needs it. · 扔石听声 (cave-stone) cut 10-16 (doc/games.md: one decision, the how-line named the sound): the passage is whole again and 喂饼 is the scene's one board.
